newsitem.title: UK: Depressed? Well they're all out to get you, too.
newsitem.headline: Depressed? Well they're all out to get you, too.

text.p: Depressed people may be nearly as paranoid as those diagnosed with clinical paranoia, British psychologists reported on Friday.

And standard psychological theories that paranoia is a defence against depression may have it all wrong, psychologists Ed Miller and Polly Karoni of the University of Leicester told a meeting of the British Psychological Society.

They were checking out this thesis on four groups of 15 volunteers each. One group was clinically depressed, one was made up of schizophrenics, one group had paranoid delusions and a control group consisted of healthy volunteers.
They were asked to imagine a series of incidents matched by age, sex and other factors with the others.

"The typical vignette was 'imagine you've gone into a shop and bought two or three small items, and you pay with a five pound note. As you leave the store you count your change and notice you have less change than you expected'," Miller said in an interview before the conference, in Edinburgh.

The volunteers were then offered four alternatives -- that being short-changed was an honest mistake, that perhaps the shopkeeper was distracted and miscounted, that the shopkeeper deliberately cheated or that the volunteer was mistaken and the change was correct.
"Depressed subjects have been shown in other work to go for the self-blame reaction. But not in this one," Miller said.
"The depressed group interpreted these negative events in a paranoid way, much more than the schizophrenic or normal control groups."
Miller said his team would now try the experiment with a slightly different slant to see if they got the same results.
He said it was not surprising that the paranoid group saw bad intentions in the scenarios.

"Usually people with paranoid delusions...are way beyond normal suspicious behaviour. They actually think the person walking behind them on the street is really following them. This suggests that the paranoid group will see malevolence in anything that's going on."

It was possible, he said, that self-esteem was still important in the behaviour of depressed people. They could feel they deserved to be cheated, mistreated or abused, while those suffering paranoid delusions could see the same situation as unjust persecution.
